title: Identical foraminiferal forms may have arisen independently again and again

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Identical foraminiferal forms may have arisen independently again and again

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The possible lines of variation in Foraminifera may be so narrow and determinate that identical forms have arisen independently many times.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: It invites one also to contemplate the possibility of the lines of possible variation being here so narrow and determinate that identical forms may have come independently into being again and again.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XII, “The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera”; topic “Conclusion: evolution of foraminiferal form”. Scope: Foraminifera through geological time

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch12-11: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.64

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Convergence is testable when morphology is mapped onto a phylogeny inferred from independent characters. Existing data can establish examples but likely cannot estimate how often it happened across all Foraminifera.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Map quantified shell forms onto independently inferred molecular and fossil phylogenies and count repeated origins of near-identical morphologies. Multiple distant lineages converging beyond uncertainty would support the claim; forms restricted to single clades would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Sparse molecular sampling and uncertain fossil placement.

Identical form requires an explicit morphometric tolerance.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Independent origin of the same shell is a phylogenetic count, and public sequences plus fossil occurrences make that count possible for planktonic and some benthic forms. Coverage through geological time is uneven, and shape-based taxonomy can manufacture both false convergence and false continuity. The result would be informative where molecules and morphology have both been recorded, and only suggestive for the rest of the order.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Place shell-shape classes on molecular and stratigraphic trees and count independent origins of the same form. Repeated origins of indistinguishable tests in distant clades or separated time intervals would support the claim; a single origin for each form, with similarity tracking relatedness, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Molecular trees are dense for planktonic clades and sparse for the long-ranging benthic groups.

Many benthic genera are still classified by the shell form whose homology is in question.
